title: Trump Administration Pushes to Open 401(k) Plans to Private Equity and Crypto
excerpt: A proposed Labor Department rule would create a legal safe harbor for employers to include alternative investments like private equity, hedge funds, and cryptocurrency in worker retirement accounts.
body:
• The Department of Labor proposed a rule in March that would create a safe harbor for employers to add alternative investments — including private equity, crypto, and hedge funds — to 401(k) plans
  • The proposal follows President Trump's August 2025 executive order directing federal agencies to expand access to alternative assets in retirement plans
  • If finalized, the rule could reshape a retirement investment market worth nearly $14 trillion
  • Critics, including Senator Elizabeth Warren, warn the rule could expose workers to higher risks, fees, and potential losses
  • Employers are not required to add alternative investments and would still need to meet strict fiduciary standards

A New Rule for Retirement Savings

The U.S. Department of Labor proposed a rule on March 31 that would make it significantly easier for 401(k) plan sponsors to include alternative investments — such as private equity, cryptocurrency, real estate, and hedge funds — on the menu of options available to workers, according to Bloomberg.

The proposed rule establishes a legal safe harbor for fiduciaries who want to add these assets, requiring them to evaluate six factors: performance, fees, liquidity, valuation, performance benchmarks, and complexity. If employers follow that process, they would be shielded from some of the litigation risk that has historically kept alternative investments out of most retirement plans, according to CNN.

"The department's days of picking winners and losers are over. Our rule clearly spells out that managers must evaluate any and all potential product offerings by following a prudent process."

— Keith Sonderling, Deputy Secretary of Labor

From Executive Order to Proposed Rule

The proposal is the culmination of a process that began with President Trump's August 2025 executive order directing the Labor Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission to facilitate expanded access to alternative assets in employer-sponsored retirement plans, according to CoinDesk.

Shortly after the executive order, the DOL's Employee Benefits Security Administration rescinded Biden-era guidance that had urged fiduciaries to exercise "extreme care" before adding crypto to retirement plans and had cautioned against private-market investments due to valuation risks and illiquidity, according to Bloomberg.

The proposed rule completed its White House regulatory review in early 2026 and was published with a 60-day public comment period, according to Bloomberg Tax.

What It Means for Workers

If finalized, the rule would open up a retirement market worth nearly $14 trillion to Wall Street firms that have long sought access to these savings. U.S. 401(k) plans hold trillions of dollars, and even a small allocation shift could send significant new capital into private equity and crypto markets. CoinDesk noted that if a large plan allocated just 1% of its portfolio to bitcoin, it could mean millions of dollars flowing into crypto funds.

However, employers are not required to offer alternative investments — the rule simply makes it legally safer for those who choose to do so. Workers would still select from whatever menu their employer provides.

Analysts at TD Cowen cautioned that real impact could be years away. "We remain skeptical that this will encourage fiduciaries to include alternatives in 401(k) plans until the courts have concurred that this language protects advisors from litigation," financial services analyst Jaret Seiberg wrote, according to CNN.

Critics Sound the Alarm

The proposal has drawn sharp criticism from lawmakers and consumer advocates. Senator Elizabeth Warren said the rule could expose workers to losses while benefiting large financial firms.

"As cracks emerge in the private credit market, private equity returns fall to 16-year lows, and crypto keeps tumbling, President Trump has decided now is the time to stick all of these risky assets into Americans' 401(k)s."

— Senator Elizabeth Warren

ProPublica reporting highlighted by NPR described the push as an effort to "weaken the main protection workers have over their retirement money," noting that private equity, hedge funds, and cryptocurrency are less regulated and often riskier than the stocks, bonds, and exchange-traded funds that currently dominate 401(k) menus.

Lisa Gomez, who served as assistant secretary of labor for employee benefits security during the Biden administration, offered a more measured view, telling CNN that fiduciaries "don't need permission to consider different types of investments" but "need clarity on how to do it prudently."

What's Next

The proposed rule may take months to finalize. If adopted, it would mark the most significant change to 401(k) investment rules in decades, potentially allowing private equity and crypto to become standard options alongside index funds and target-date funds in worker retirement accounts.

For now, no changes have taken effect, and workers' existing 401(k) allocations are unaffected. The debate is likely to intensify as the rule moves through the finalization process and the 2028 election cycle brings retirement policy into sharper political focus.
